question: The money: what is the dollar on the chain, who owes it, and what backs it?
answer: This page reads every crypto dollar the library tracks: 36 coins and tokens (17 of them payment stablecoins or candidates), each with its exact issuing company, legal route, reserves and who holds them, attestation, redemption terms, size, freeze power (33 can freeze) and yield; then the July card decks that first mapped issuers, DeFi dollars, company control and GENIUS events; the Crypto Hub's 54 cash-leg nodes, which separate a stablecoin from a bank deposit and from central-bank money; and the dated filings and central-bank digital money moves. Who owes the dollar is always a named legal entity, not a brand or a chain.

rows.title: USDC · USD Coin
fields: Circle Internet Financial, LLC (outside the European Economic Area); Circle Internet Financial Europe SAS (inside the EEA)
Circle; distributed widely by exchanges and wallets, notably Coinbase
United States (Circle Internet Financial, LLC); France / EEA (Circle Internet Financial Europe SAS)

Circle's stated plan is to move U.S. issuance to a New York trust company (now chartered by NYDFS), but the October 15, 2026 USDC Terms still name Circle Internet Financial, LLC, and a state issuer above $10 billion outstanding must move to federal oversight within 360 days unless waived (Sec. 4(d)).

Circle Internet Trust Company LLC (doing business as Circle New York Trust) received a New York limited-purpose trust charter from NYDFS, announced July 31, 2026. Separately, Circle National Trust (First National Digital Currency Bank, N.A.) got final OCC approval July 10, 2026 and its charter took effect July 24, 2026; it does custody and trust work and does not issue USDC. Neither entity is the USDC issuer under the current terms.

Composition: Mostly shares of the Circle Reserve Fund (USDXX), which can hold cash, short-dated U.S. Treasuries and overnight Treasury repurchase agreements; the rest is cash, mostly at a handful of the world's largest banks.
Custodians: BlackRock (manages the Circle Reserve Fund), BNY (primary reserve custodian per library July 2026 cards; not named on the current transparency page)
Latest attestation: By: A Big Four accounting firm (not named on Circle's page); Date: 2026-08

Direct 1:1 redemption only for holders with a Circle Mint account who pass identity checks (in practice institutions); less fees in Circle's fee schedule. Everyone else sells or redeems through an exchange, wallet or other intermediary.
Basis: USDC in circulation, rounded on Circle's page (Circle's Aug 31 attestation: 73,320,757,305)
Ethereum, Solana, Avalanche C-Chain, Stellar, Hedera, Algorand, XDC, Arc (used to pay network fees)

How: Circle may block addresses and freeze USDC, temporarily or permanently, that it believes is tied to illegal activity or terms violations, and acts on legal orders from government authorities (USDC Terms, Section 13).

BNY's reserve-custody role is in the July library cards but not on the current transparency page; confirm.
Full chain list not compiled; the list above is only chains named in the library.

Where reserve income goes: To Circle. USDC Terms say USDC itself pays holders nothing and holders have no right to reserve income. Circle reported $652.5 million of reserve income in Q1 2026 against $41.6 million of other revenue, and pays a large share to distributors: $324.6 million to Coinbase in Q2 2026.
Rewards via third parties: Coinbase runs USDC Rewards, which it calls 'a loyalty program funded by Coinbase'; in the U.S. it requires a paid Coinbase One membership and the rate is set by Coinbase.

Genius bearing: Section 4(a)(11) bars the issuer from paying holders interest or yield solely for holding, using or keeping the coin; it takes effect with the Act (January 18, 2027 per the genius_act_milestones master). The OCC's proposed rule (not final) would presume the issuer is paying holders when it has an arrangement with an affiliate or related third party that in turn pays holders; whether that reaches Circle's revenue sharing with Coinbase has not been decided.

Circle Technology Services runs CPN technology without becoming the principal party to transactions., Its money products, USDC and EURC are payment coins. USYC is a token for fund shares. sections.sub: The GENIUS Act does not make a blockchain or wallet legal. It makes a specific issuer, with specific reserves and terms, eligible to issue in the U.S. Later, it lets U.S. platforms keep distributing that issuer's coin. rows.title: Circle plans to move USDC to a new New York issuer and its reserves to a new federal trust bank
fields: Live with current issuer · planned move to a New York issuer · federal trust bank for reserves

Circle Internet Financial, LLC is still the issuer outside the European Economic Area (EEA). Circle told the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) it plans to move USDC issuance to a separate company. That company is Circle Internet Trust Company, LLC, a proposed New York limited-purpose trust. Circle Internet Financial Europe SAS remains the EEA issuer.

Eligible Circle Mint customers can create and redeem USDC 1:1. A holder gets a direct claim only by becoming an eligible Mint customer. Individuals generally get USDC through wallets, exchanges and neobanks.
Highly liquid dollar reserves, held separately for holders: bank deposits, short-dated Treasuries and overnight Treasury repo. Most are held through the Circle Reserve Fund, managed by BlackRock.

The asset types closely match the GENIUS Act's list. But no public determination exists that the reserves meet the rules for a permitted payment stablecoin issuer (PPSI). Circle's own disclosure is still the evidence.

BlackRock manages the Circle Reserve Fund, and BNY is the primary reserve custodian. Circle National Trust is designed to manage reserves, act as collateral trustee and hold digital assets in the future. It expressly does not issue USDC.
Direct 1:1 redemption is for institutions, through Circle Mint. Everyday holders normally sell or redeem through an intermediary.
Wallets, exchanges, banks, card networks and payment processors already distribute USDC widely. The companies that connect USDC to these systems are already established.

Circle's stated plan is a real change of issuer, to Circle Internet Trust Company, LLC. That company would then seek approval as a State-qualified PPSI under a New York regime certified under GENIUS. Using today's issuer, CIF LLC, as a federal nonbank issuer is only a fallback if the plan changes.

Circle Internet Trust needs a charter and stablecoin approval from the New York State Department of Financial Services (NYDFS). It also needs the required GENIUS state certification and issuer approval. Circle must then sign an assignment and assumption or new terms. Token administration, reserve-control agreements and attestations must move to the new issuer.
If the issuer becomes permitted, U.S. digital-asset service providers can keep offering the coin. Existing integrations do not by themselves meet the issuer requirement.
USDC already places the money behind circulating coins in deposits, Treasury bills and Treasury repo. GENIUS would standardize this flow from private dollar tokens into government debt.

Circle National Trust is not the planned issuer. Circle Internet Trust Company, LLC is a separate proposed New York company. We found no operative novation (legal transfer of the obligations) and no New York approval.

rows.title: Whether a token is a payment stablecoin depends on how it is redeemed, not on its $1 price
fields: law enacted · how it applies to these tokens is not settled
A payment stablecoin must have an issuer obligated to convert, redeem or buy it back for a fixed amount of money.
The law separately requires the issuer to promise, or create a reasonable expectation of, a stable value.
Who exactly the legal issuer is, and what the holder receives on redemption
A token qualifies only if it is built for payment or settlement, an issuer must redeem it, and redemption is for a fixed amount of money. Deposits and securities are excluded.
What backs a token does not, by itself, decide whether it qualifies.
Redeeming for cash or a bank deposit differs from receiving USDC or one dollar's worth of crypto.
A software swap, a peg stability module (PSM, a contract that swaps the token for another stablecoin) or a collateral redemption is not automatically a legal person's promise to pay money.
A permitted or recognized issuer may not pay yield just for holding, using or keeping the coin.
Issuer supervision, and the technical ability to obey lawful orders such as freezes, apply only once the product counts as a payment stablecoin.
Each DeFi token must be tested against every part of the definition. Calling it a 'stablecoin' does not make it one.
Falling outside the definition may avoid some GENIUS rules. It does not give the token the approval a permitted payment stablecoin issuer (PPSI) holds.
Payment processors will likely prefer the coin whose issuer and redemption rights are easiest to certify.
Treating a $1 price-feed (oracle) target or a USDC swap as dollar redemption under the law.
Falling outside GENIUS does not mean unregulated. Securities, commodities, lending, sanctions and other laws still apply.

rows.title: Circle starts from its regulated USDC coin and is expanding into payments, a blockchain and patents
fields: USDC live · move to a U.S. issuer not finished · IBM patents acquired
USDC and EURC, CCTP (Cross-Chain Transfer Protocol), Gateway, CPN (Circle Payments Network), wallet tools, Arc development, USYC administration and a newly acquired IBM blockchain patent portfolio.
Issuer liability to holders, moving coins between blockchains, institutional settlement and its own purpose-built blockchain
Who can mint or redeem, supported blockchains, token addresses and compliance actions. Separate processors and blockchains keep their own approvals.

Circle Internet Group, Inc. is the public parent. Circle Internet Financial, LLC is the current issuer outside the European Economic Area (EEA); Circle Internet Financial Europe SAS is the EEA issuer. The proposed Circle Internet Trust Company is the intended New York issuer. Circle National Trust has final approval from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) as a separate custody and trust company that does not issue coins. Circle Technology Services runs CPN technology without becoming the principal party to transactions.
USDC and EURC are payment coins. USYC is a token for fund shares. The Arc network's asset and its infrastructure are separate things.

Reserve income makes up most revenue. Circle reported Q1 2026 reserve income of $652.5 million versus $41.6 million of other revenue. It also reported $405.4 million of distribution and transaction costs, including large payments to distributors. Platform, network, fund and future Arc income are secondary.
Issuer contracts, token-admin functions, Circle Mint onboarding, CCTP and Gateway support, CPN participation and the Arc roadmap.
Circle relies on the BlackRock-managed Circle Reserve Fund, BNY as custodian, partner banks, supported blockchains, distributors such as Coinbase and Binance, and payment processors.
USDC is the leading regulated base coin under exchanges, DeFi (decentralized finance) collateral, vaults and merchant payment services.
Merchants can accept USDC directly through processors. USDC can also settle or pay out behind a familiar checkout without the shopper seeing it.
Strong chance of approval under the GENIUS Act. But the exact move to a U.S. issuer and product-specific approval are separate legal steps.

Circle National Trust received final OCC approval on 2026-07-10, but it is not the issuer. Circle acquired the IBM patent portfolio on 2026-07-27; we have not found a public list of the patents. The proposed New York issuer and the transfer of USDC contracts to it (novation) are not yet proven.
Which IBM patents cover bank integration, settlement among approved parties only, or enterprise controls? When will New York issuer terms line up with Arc and CPN production?
A reserve-bank or custodian problem, an outage in issuer access, a token-admin error, a bridge or routing failure, or a mismatch when legal duties move to a new issuer.
Buying IBM's blockchain patent portfolio did not give Circle COBOL, IBM mainframes or bank customer systems.

Trading and custody fees, subscriptions and services, USDC-related income, payment infrastructure and activity tied to Base.
Customer identity checks (KYC), supported assets, custody keys, merchant APIs and Base transaction ordering. Anyone can submit Base fault proofs, but upgrades need 9 of 12 Security Council members.

A major holder and router of USDC. Links stablecoins to trading, DeFi (decentralized finance) on Base, institutional custody and payments by AI agents.
Coinbase Payments handles acceptance. Processors such as Checkout.com or PPRO keep the merchant relationship and the contract to settle in regular money.
Likely a critical digital-asset service provider and distributor, even when it is not the issuer.
Coinbase announced merchant acceptance and enterprise payouts as live for eligible users. Headline volume and Base figures are company-reported.
In each processor integration, who exactly is responsible for compliance, conversion, custody and refunds? What is the status of the proposed trust company?
One platform outage can hit transfers, card transactions and onchain services at the same time. A failure in Base's sequencer or in custody would hit many services at once.
Stablecoin volume on Base is not Coinbase revenue, USDC in circulation or merchant-payment volume. Open fault proofs do not remove Coinbase's control of the sequencer and interface.

Payments software, a central place in the XRP Ledger (XRPL) ecosystem, Standard Custody, Ripple Custody, Ripple Prime, Ripple Treasury and acquired wallet and payment systems.
Issuing a stablecoin, custody, prime brokerage, connecting corporate treasuries and routing institutional payments

Standard Custody controls RLUSD issuance and redemption. It can freeze, blacklist, burn or replace tokens and suspend redemptions. Product subsidiaries control access to custody, prime and treasury services. XRPL validators keep their network roles.

Ripple Labs Inc. is separate from Standard Custody & Trust Company, which issues RLUSD today. Ripple National Trust has only preliminary, conditional approval. Hidden Road Partners CIV US LLC—not Ripple Labs—holds the relevant memberships in FICC (Fixed Income Clearing Corporation) and DTC (Depository Trust Company). The Metaco/Palisade, Rail and GTreasury entities keep the specific roles they had when acquired.
RLUSD (owed by its issuer), XRP (the ledger's native asset), third-party assets issued on XRPL, and customer securities and collateral are legally separate.
Payments, custody and software fees; prime brokerage and financing; treasury software; XRP holdings and markets; and RLUSD-related business.
RLUSD token administration, customer onboarding, custody policies, prime-brokerage collateral, software integration, and market memberships held by specific acquired subsidiaries.
BNY for reserve custody and banking, other banks and exchanges, the specific subsidiaries that are DTC and FICC members, XRPL validators and outside blockchains such as Ethereum.
RLUSD is a regulated base coin for tokenized funds, DeFi (decentralized finance) and Ripple Payments. USDC also exists natively on XRPL.
Ripple Payments and the acquired Rail systems can convert between stablecoins and regular money. Evidence of direct use at consumer checkout terminals is more limited.
RLUSD likely seeks approval as a state-qualified issuer through Standard Custody. Ripple National Trust is on a separate timeline.

Standard Custody issuance, Ripple Prime, Ripple Treasury and Ripple Custody are live. Ripple National Trust has only preliminary, conditional approval. The deciding proof is repeated transactions that use several acquired businesses together.
Which acquired connections become Ripple's own production systems? Does post-trade activity actually move to XRPL?
Too many services concentrated in one corporate group, a custodian or issuer failure, losses at the prime broker, a token-admin action, or a ledger or bridge incident.
A subsidiary's connection to DTC, FICC, Swift, Canton or a bank does not prove that institutions have adopted XRP, XRPL or RippleNet.

Offshore USD₮ and U.S. USA₮ share a brand but not an issuer, reserve or legal promise.
Reserve income, returns on its investment portfolio, issuance and redemption relationships, and group investments.
Token freeze and burn, primary minting and redemption only after know-your-customer (KYC) checks, choice of blockchains, self-custody wallet distribution and reserve allocation.
Banks, custodians, primary dealers, exchanges, blockchains and—only for USA₮—Anchorage and its reserve trust.

It usually reaches merchants through conversion at an exchange, wallet or processor, not through direct retail redemption.
Offshore USD₮ needs a foreign-issuer approval path or limits on its distribution. USA₮ is a separate regulated U.S. option.
Watch whether U.S. access moves to USA₮ while global trading stays in USD₮.
For each product: its exact status under GENIUS, its U.S. distribution policy and its reserve and custody details.
Losses at reserves or custodians, exchange delisting, a redemption backlog, a mismatch between legal entities, or token controls on a specific blockchain.
USA₮'s Anchorage and Cantor structure does not apply to USD₮.

Issuing coins under other brands (white-label), running reserves and redemptions, and branded consumer access

Reserve income, fees for issuance, tokenization and settlement, and deals that share earnings with distributors. PayPal Digital separately runs a PYUSD rewards program with a variable rate, paid in PYUSD.
Issuer terms, reserve accounts, token administration, who qualifies for a direct account, and distribution contracts.
Banks and custodians holding reserves, PayPal and other distributors, supported blockchains and payment networks.
Paxos coins can move into wallets, exchanges and DeFi (decentralized finance), while Paxos remains the place to redeem.

Paxos is well prepared to be an issuer. Product-specific approvals and the treatment of distributor payments remain open.
Current terms dated 2026-06-30 name the issuing entities. Moving PayPal customer contracts did not change the issuer.
How the limits on issuers paying yield treat Paxos's shared earnings and PayPal Digital's balance-based rewards. Which Paxos entity serves each jurisdiction.
Losses at the issuer or custodian, a distributor dropping the product, a blockchain admin action, or confusing the brand with the company that owes holders.
PayPal does not owe PYUSD redemption just because the token carries its brand.

Merchant acceptance, conversion to regular money, in-app wallets, branded coin issuance, cards and platform accounts
Which merchants and payments qualify, wallet setup, supported assets, conversion paths, the card program and regional access.

USDC, EURC, and Bridge-issued or custom stablecoins. A Morpho position is a separate DeFi (decentralized finance) claim. A card transaction remains a card-network obligation.
Payment processing, currency exchange and payment routing, issuing, financial accounts, platform services and acquired systems.
Dashboard and API access, identity checks (KYC), who holds wallet keys, which issuer is used, supported payment paths and card approvals.
Banks, card networks, blockchains, Bridge's bank-payment connections, licensed custodians and Morpho vault liquidity.
Links balances to branded coins, in-app wallets and Morpho yield picked by curators.
A stablecoin balance or DeFi-funded wallet can pay through a regular card or Stripe checkout, while the merchant receives ordinary settlement.
The issuer depends on the product. Stripe or Bridge may be distributor, payment router, issuer or program manager in different flows.
Bridge, Privy and some stablecoin products are live. Tempo had a public test network. Stripe's Sessions 2026 announcements list generally available (GA), preview and future-quarter items separately.
Who exactly issues and holds custody for each custom coin? How do liquidation and credit work when someone spends from a DeFi position?
One outage hitting payments, wallets and routing at once, a sponsor-bank failure, a smart-contract loss, or unclear treatment of who owns customer property.
A roadmap item is not a live product. Bridge routing payments does not automatically mean Bridge issued the coin.

rows.title: Ethereum hosts stablecoins and other financial tokens but is not their issuer
fields: live · several independent software clients · community-governed

No single body owns Ethereum. The Ethereum Foundation, software client teams, validators, node operators, standards authors, infrastructure firms and layer-2 (L2) network operators have different roles.
Running and settling transactions, smart-contract records and apps that plug into each other
Validators can censor transactions or leave them out. Client teams and the community can choose software and recovery plans. Application admins keep their own keys.

The Ethereum Foundation is a Swiss Stiftung (foundation) and an influential funder and organizer. It is not the protocol, the validators or an issuer. Consensys Software Inc. runs products such as MetaMask and Infura and contributes client software, but it does not own Ethereum.
ETH pays transaction fees (gas) and secures consensus. USDC, PYUSD, USDe, GHO and tokenized securities are liabilities or claims of other systems.
ETH fees and burn, validator rewards and MEV (profit from ordering transactions), L2 income, RPC and wallet services, and application fees.
EIP (Ethereum Improvement Proposal) debate, AllCoreDevs coordination, independent client builds, node and validator adoption, rare community-led recovery, and app and L2 upgrade keys.
Client diversity, validator concentration, RPC access, bridges and L2s, oracles (outside data feeds), app admins and stablecoin issuers.
The main network where issuer coins, lending, decentralized exchanges (DEXs), synthetic dollars, vaults and tokenized assets work together.
Usually through L2s, wallets, processors or crypto-linked cards, not direct retail use of the base layer-1 (L1) chain.
The network does not decide whether a coin is a payment stablecoin. The exact issuer and its redemption promise do.
Protocol upgrades need client teams to build them and validators and nodes to adopt them. No single company controls every layer.
In practice, how concentrated are clients, staking providers, RPC providers, L2 sequencers and stablecoin admins?
Client bug, validator concentration, finality failure, community split, L2 or bridge failure, or a compromised app admin.
The Ethereum Foundation (EF) does not own Ethereum, and Consensys does not control it. Validators do not formally vote on every EIP. Stablecoin value does not become EF revenue or liability.

rows.title: Stellar treats reaching users, not the token, as the main constraint
fields: cash conversion and stablecoin payments live · DTC connection not yet live

The Stellar Development Foundation (SDF) supports protocol development and ecosystem programs. Third-party issuers, anchors (cash-conversion companies), validators, wallets and MoneyGram keep separate roles.
Moving assets cheaply, standards for anchors, converting cash, and distributing regulated assets

Each issuer can set authorization, freeze or clawback-style controls on its asset. Anchors can refuse conversion. Validators choose which validators they trust (quorum sets) and vote on protocol versions and settings.
The Stellar Development Foundation is a nonprofit support body. It is not the issuer of USDC, PYUSD, MGUSD or tokenized funds.
XLM pays fees and minimum balances (reserves). Third-party stablecoins and securities keep their own legal issuers.
Users need XLM for fees, rent and minimum balances. But fees go into a fee pool no one can access, and validators receive no protocol rewards. Anchors, wallets and applications earn separately.
Protocol releases, validator quorum choices, SDF ecosystem funding, issuer settings on each asset, anchors and wallet integrations.
Issuers, the MoneyGram/Crossmint cash network, anchors, validators, wallets, card networks and a future DTC (Depository Trust Company) connection.
USDC, PYUSD and locally distributed stablecoins can connect cash, remittances, aid, wallets and tokenized assets.
MoneyGram and wallet apps convert cash to and from stablecoins. Visa/Wirex settlement and spending through apps offer other paths.
SDF is normally infrastructure, not a payment-stablecoin issuer. Each asset on Stellar needs its own legal test.
Cash conversion and payments are live. The DTC connection targets H1 2027 (first half). The Protocol 26/CAP-77 emergency ledger-key quarantine must be confirmed on mainnet before we call it live.
How wider distribution turns into lasting income for the network and token, and how issuer controls work with Soroban smart contracts.
Anchor insolvency, issuer freeze, validator quorum fault, wallet failure or trading split across too many places.
SDF is not a bank or stablecoin issuer. XLM is not reserve backing. A DTC connection does not replace DTC's own books. Validators are not paid like miners or stakers.

rows.title: Hedera offers businesses built-in tools that let issuers control their own tokens
fields: network and tools live · range of real production use still uneven
A network whose rules and ownership the Hedera Council governs, plus ecosystem tools. Stablecoin Studio is an open-source kit that third-party issuers use to issue coins.
Council-run consensus, built-in token tools, predictable fees and business workflows mixing public and private systems
The Council governs network software, treasury and pricing. Token issuers set their own keys for identity checks (KYC), freezing, pausing, wiping balances and supply.

Hedera Hashgraph, LLC dba (doing business as) Hedera Council is the Delaware entity that governs the network. Hedera Foundation and Hashgraph are independent ecosystem and software organizations. Hiero is the open-source project. All are separate from token issuers.
HBAR pays public-network fees and secures consensus. Stablecoins, tokenized collateral and state-issued tokens are claims on third parties.
Network fees paid in HBAR and ecosystem activity. Issuers and applications earn separately.

Council decisions govern treasury, pricing, membership, releases and mainnet-node policy. Only Council members currently run mainnet consensus nodes. Each token is controlled by keys its issuer sets in the Hedera Token Service (HTS): admin, supply, KYC, freeze, wipe, fee and pause.
Council continuity, nodes, outside issuers, custodians, reserve-data providers and oracles (outside data feeds) such as Chainlink.
Stablecoin Studio provides connection points for compliance and proof of reserves. Hedera Token Service provides built-in controls over a token's whole life.
Issuer and payment-provider apps can use Hedera. Merchant acceptance still runs through wallets, processors and acquirers (merchants' payment banks).
Stablecoin Studio may help an issuer meet control rules. It cannot supply the legal issuer, rights to reserves or approval.
Wyoming FRNT and commercial projects show real deployment. Institutional pilots still need confirmation that they are in production.
Which uses repeat at scale, and how public Hedera connects with private HashSphere networks.
Council or node concentration, stolen keys, an issuer-admin action, an oracle or custody fault, or private and public networks falling out of sync.
Open-source Hiero code does not let anyone join mainnet without approval. Council governance does not make Hedera the issuer of every token made with its tools.

rows.title: Chainlink's data and cross-chain messages can affect settlement, but it owns no asset
fields: data-feed (oracle) and CCIP services live · rules for institutional use incomplete
Software, standards and business relationships for data feeds, proof of reserve, CCIP (Cross-Chain Interoperability Protocol) and automated workflows.
Verified data, messages between blockchains and transactions that run only when conditions are met

Each service's proxy owners and admins, DON (decentralized oracle network) settings, CCIP rate limits and emergency controls can halt or change a service. Chainlink does not usually control the reserve or the official record of the asset.
Chainlink Labs and the ecosystem and foundation bodies are separate from independent node operators and customer protocols.
LINK pays for and backs parts of the service economics. Assets arriving on another chain remain issuer or protocol claims.

Service fees, the option to pay in other tokens that convert to LINK, and the Chainlink Reserve, plus limited staking and security mechanisms. Official v0.2 staking has a 45 million LINK cap and launched around the Ethereum ETH/USD feed—not every Chainlink service.
Service settings, which nodes and operators serve, data sources, CCIP routes between chains, emergency procedures and customer integration contracts.
Data providers, node operators, sending and receiving blockchains, protocol admins and institutional counterparties.
Prices collateral, supports proof-of-reserve designs and moves instructions and tokens between blockchains, including GHO routes and RLUSD data.
Indirect. It supports reliable conversion, risk checks and cross-chain settlement that wallets and processors use.
Likely an intermediary or service provider, not an issuer. Legal duties depend on the exact service and its control over transfers.
It is used in production. But public terms on liability, corrections and recovery for institutional workflows remain limited.
Which services staking secures, who bears losses from bad data, and how corrections for institutions are decided.
Wrong or outdated data, nodes colluding, a cross-chain hack, a misconfigured route or unclear liability.
An oracle integration is not issuance or custody. LINK does not back stablecoins moved between chains. Staking does not currently secure every service.

rows.title: Fireblocks controls how institutions move crypto, though money does not always pass through it
fields: Wallet and key management, software that enforces transfer rules, network connections, payment tools and DeFi (decentralized finance) access products for institutions.
Keys, transfer rules, checking counterparties, approving workflows and connections
Rules the customer sets can approve or block transfers. Fireblocks says some of its products do not put it in the flow of funds.
The software and service company, its trust and custody offerings, and the customer's custodians must be identified for each contract.
Fireblocks supports many third-party coins and protocol receipts. Supporting them does not move issuance or reserve liability to Fireblocks.
Fees for enterprise software and platform use, custody, and network and payment services.
Key workflows using MPC (multi-party computation, which splits keys), approved address lists, approval rules, wallet verification and supported integrations.
Licensed customers, custodians, blockchains, swap and bridge protocols, and DeFi contracts.
Moves institutional balances into stablecoin settlement and products such as Aave/Morpho Earn, while the coin's issuer stays separate.
A processor or payment service provider (PSP) can use Fireblocks for wallets and settlement while keeping its own licenses and merchant contracts.
May count as a digital-asset service provider. Exact status depends on its role in custody, transfers and the flow of funds.
Fireblocks Earn became generally available in April 2026. Flow launched 2026-07-27. Technical support or a launch does not prove customer use or volume.
Which entity acts, and who holds custody, in each flow? Who recovers funds and who is liable after a rule or key failure?
Stolen keys or tampered rules, a service outage, a hacked integration, or a counterparty or blockchain failure.
Supporting an asset does not make Fireblocks its issuer, reserve custodian or principal party to the transaction.

rows.title: Anchorage, a federally chartered bank, issues stablecoins under other companies' brands
fields: federally chartered bank · issues several stablecoins
The Anchorage Digital Bank charter, a custody platform, and a way of issuing stablecoins that uses a separate reserve trust for each product.
Custody, issuance, reserve trusts and redemption for institutions, all under a federal bank charter
Under product terms, the bank can refuse minting or redemption, freeze, block, seize or migrate tokens, and restrict accounts.

Anchor Labs is the parent. Anchorage Digital Bank, N.A. issues the coins. Separate South Dakota reserve trusts own the assets. Anchorage Digital Neo Ltd. and other affiliates may pay rewards or provide separate services.
USDtb, USA₮ and USDGO are separate debts to holders, each with its own trust. USDPT is listed or planned, but evidence of its first mint and attestation still needs confirming.
Custody and issuance fees, pay for managing reserves as a fiduciary, and platform services. Affiliates that pay rewards are separate.
Issuer onboarding, trust management, token administration, custody and agreements with the brands.
Reserve custodians and assets, brand partners such as Ethena and Tether, institutional clients and supported blockchains.
Lets DeFi and crypto brands keep reaching their customers while a federal bank is the legal issuer and sets the reserve rules.
The coins can move into wallets and processors. Ordinary holders may need to be onboarded before redeeming directly with the bank.
A strong permitted-issuer candidate. It still needs product-specific approvals and review of its reward programs.
The bank says it currently issues several coins. Fourth-party programs and wider distribution are on separate timelines.
Product-specific approvals as a permitted payment stablecoin issuer (PPSI), reserve holdings and exact treatment of affiliate rewards.
A bank or operational failure, a reserve-trust problem, a brand dropping its coin, a token-admin action, or limited access to direct redemption.
The brand partner is not the issuer. A reward from an affiliate is not automatically yield paid by the bank.

rows.title: Aave DAO controls GHO by deciding who may mint it and how much
fields: No ordinary parent owns the protocol. Aave DAO (decentralized autonomous organization, run by token votes) governs deployments and GHO; Aave Labs builds software and interfaces.
Collateral-backed loans, liquidity and how much GHO each approved minter (facilitator) may create
Governance can add or remove facilitators and change caps. Stewards can adjust rates, exposures and freezes within limits governance gave them.

Aave DAO and community, Aave Labs (with its interface and trademark roles), independent risk and technical service providers, stewards and GHO facilitators are different actors. Aave Labs' terms deny that it controls the protocol.
GHO is the protocol dollar and sGHO its savings receipt. Aave also has deposit and debt tokens and the AAVE governance token.
Borrowing interest, protocol fees, liquidation income and GHO revenue directed to the DAO-controlled treasury.
Governance executors, each facilitator's mint limit (bucket), guardians, stewards with limited powers, risk providers, oracle choices and Aave Labs' interface policies.
Collateral, Chainlink and other oracles (price-data services), liquidators, governance voting, service providers and stablecoin liquidity.
GHO is a dollar the DAO controls. Aave also provides the lending and yield underneath regulated coins.
Most likely a wallet or processor converts GHO, or a card service lets someone spend against an Aave or Morpho position.
Strong argument that GHO is not a payment stablecoin, since no named company owes fiat redemption. Approval for institutional use remains uncertain.
RemoteGSM (remote GHO Stability Module) and a modular design spread GHO across more chains; minting still comes only from governance-approved sources.
Whether the DAO is treated as a person or issuer, facilitators' legal liability, and processor acceptance.
An oracle or collateral shock, a takeover of governance, a facilitator fault, failed liquidations or a smart-contract exploit.
Aave Labs is not automatically the issuer or operator of every DAO deployment.

rows.title: Sky calls its dollars a 'protocol obligation,' but no clear legal entity owes holders
fields: DAI, USDS and sUSDS live · who the issuer is remains unresolved

Sky governance controls collateral, rates, PSMs (peg stability modules), how executive decisions are carried out, and the upgradeable USDS contracts. Ecosystem entities provide interfaces and support.
Which collateral is accepted, how many dollars exist, the savings rate and the move to the new protocol
Governance can change settings and contract code. Interfaces can restrict users. Collateral custodians keep their own controls over each asset.

Sky governance controls the protocol. Skybase International provides an interface and says it is not the issuer or operator. Sky Frontier Foundation, Agents such as Spark and Grove, and collateral SPVs (special purpose vehicles) and other entities are separate; do not treat them as one.
DAI and USDS are protocol dollars. sUSDS and the DSR (Dai Savings Rate) are separate savings claims. Collateral includes crypto, stablecoins and RWAs (real-world assets).
Lending and RWA investments produce protocol income. That income pays savings rates, rewards, expenses and token buybacks.
Executive votes and the code they run (spells), token upgrades, PSMs, rates, Agents and interface terms.
USDC and other collateral issuers, oracles, custodians, governance voting, market liquidity and front ends.
One of the most liquid protocol-dollar and DeFi (decentralized finance) collateral systems. USDS seeks wider use of regulated assets.
DAI and USDS can be distributed or converted. But a processor supporting them does not create a company that owes holders regular money.
Likely not a payment stablecoin. Ambiguity comes from Sky's official 'protocol obligation' language and the law's broad definition of a person.
The move from DAI to USDS changes the economics, who controls it and its legal identity.
Whether the law treats the DAO or governance as an issuer or person, and which entity owns specific RWA claims.
Collateral losing its peg, governance takeover, an oracle or PSM failure, a custodian or SPV problem, or a contract migration error.
Swapping for USDC is not necessarily redemption for monetary value as the law defines it.

rows.title: Curve has no ordinary issuer, but the contract that mints crvUSD is easy to identify
fields: Curve DAO governs market-creating contracts (factories), markets, debt ceilings and fee routing. Swiss Stake is a development body, not a documented company that owes holders regular money.
Stablecoin swap liquidity, crvUSD minting, and the peg and liquidation mechanisms
The DAO can change future markets, caps and fees. The contracts and templates set what can change after launch.
Curve DAO and its governance; Swiss Stake AG, where development, research, security and interface work is concentrated; token contracts; gauges; oracles; and Peg Keepers are separate actors.
crvUSD is a protocol debt asset, scrvUSD is a vault share and CRV is the governance and incentive token.
Admin fees on trading, lending and crvUSD interest, gauge rewards and vault revenue sharing. Swiss Stake also has proposed earnings from its interface.
ControllerFactory's power to mint, DAO votes, debt ceilings, fee-splitting contracts, oracles and liquidity rewards.
Outside collateral, oracles and market liquidity, liquidators, governance and smart-contract security.
A dollar created inside the protocol and a core source of liquidity. scrvUSD separates the base coin from savings that earn fees.
Likely converted into a payment coin a processor supports before it is spent.
Likely not a payment stablecoin, since no named company owes holders regular money. Whether the DAO or factory counts as issuer is open.
We found no regulator decision. Control is visible even where ordinary legal liability is not.
Who the law treats as issuer or person, and how markets that cannot be changed after launch affect governance's liability.
An oracle or LLAMMA (Curve's soft-liquidation system) error, collateral crash, liquidity drain, hacked factory or governance, or smart-contract exploit.
Swiss Stake's development role does not make it liable for redemption.

rows.title: Frax is trying to move issuance into a company while its DAO keeps control
fields: frxUSD live · licensing and who owes holders still in transition
Frax DAO keeps the protocol's economics and the right to override. Frax Inc. PBC (public benefit corporation) takes on delegated compliance, reserve, bank-payment and issuer functions.
Issuance shared by a company and the DAO, DAO governance, bank minting and redemption, and collateral providers built into the protocol
The company issuer can enforce identity-check (KYC) and reserve policy. The DAO can revoke or override what it delegated. Custodians control their own mint and burn processes.

Frax Inc. PBC—formerly FinresPBC—holds delegated issuer and compliance functions. Frax DAO keeps the economics and the power to revoke. Custodians and real-world-asset (RWA) providers built into the protocol, and interface entities, are separate.
frxUSD base coin, sfrxUSD wrapper, protocol collateral and partner-branded (white-label) layers.
Income from reserves and collateral, protocol fees, DeFi strategies, and income the DAO controls.
FIP (Frax Improvement Proposal) delegation, DAO override, issuer compliance, custodian choice, token administration and bank payment connections.
Licenses, banks, custodians, providers of tokenized Treasurys and other RWAs, governance and trading venues.
The clearest attempt to turn a protocol-created dollar into a coin under a regulated issuer's rules and owners.
Processors could accept it if the exact issuer, reserves and approval are certified. White-label coins may extend its reach.
A strong payment-stablecoin candidate, but not proven permitted. Rewards paid in the same token raise a yield question.
FIP-432 is a governance vote to delegate. It is not final approval or full proof of which entity legally owes holders.
Who holds final legal authority after licensing, who owns the reserves, and whether the issuer or an affiliate pays rewards.
DAO–company conflict, losses at custodians or RWA providers, licensing failure, governance takeover, or strain on the wrapper or peg.
Evidence of a regulated pivot is not a finding of completed PPSI (permitted payment stablecoin issuer) status.

rows.title: Ethena backs USDe with hedged crypto held by custodians, not a reserve account

badge.text: USDe and sUSDe live · USDtb partnership live

fields: USDe and sUSDe live · USDtb partnership live
Ethena's protocol and operating entities coordinate USDe issuance, collateral custody, derivatives hedging and the sUSDe vault. Anchorage separately issues USDtb.
Minting a synthetic dollar, hedging, holding collateral with custodians outside exchanges, and paying out yield
Access for approved Mint Users, limits on minting and redemption, blocked staking addresses and operational risk controls.

Ethena (BVI) Limited runs the application and the current USDe issuer relationship. Ethena OpCo Ltd., owned by Ethena Foundation, handles rewards, ENA distributions and sUSDe operations. 'Ethena Labs' provides research and communications. Anchorage Bank separately issues USDtb.
USDe (synthetic dollar), sUSDe (vault receipt) and USDtb (regulated reserve-backed coin) are separate.
Derivatives funding payments and basis (price-gap) income, staking and reserve income, paid out through sUSDe and ecosystem arrangements.
Mint User agreements, gatekeeper and blacklist roles, custody arrangements, how much goes to each trading venue, hedging operations, vault roles, ENA governance and Risk Committee powers.
Centralized derivatives exchanges, market makers, Copper, Ceffu and other custodians, oracle data, stablecoin collateral and liquidity.
A large synthetic dollar and yield product, and the brand partner for USDtb, which a federal bank issues.
USDe is generally converted to a payment coin or backs a card or wallet product. USDtb offers a more regulated base coin.
USDe does not neatly fit the GENIUS Act's narrow reserve and redemption rules. USDtb is analyzed with Anchorage as its issuer.
Its strength must be tested under real stress at exchanges or custodians, not only by normal attestations.
Ordinary holders' redemption rights, how concentrated the hedges are, treatment in bankruptcy and regulatory category.
Custodian or exchange default, hedges breaking down, funding rates reversing, collateral loss, or a mint-control or smart-contract failure.
Delta neutrality (hedging against price moves) is a risk-management claim, not a guarantee of redemption at par.

rows.title: Ondo's tokenized Treasury products work like cash but legally remain securities
fields: USDY and OUSG live, limited to eligible investors
Product issuers, adviser and general partner (GP) entities, token-control systems and distribution relationships for tokenized Treasury and fund products.
Issuing securities, deciding which investors qualify, controlling transfers, tokenized collateral and redemption
Approved and blocked lists, pauses on buying in and redeeming, rate limits and controlled bridges. Agents and custodians keep their own controls over the assets.

Ondo Finance Inc. runs services. Ondo Foundation is an independently governed Cayman foundation. Ondo Global Markets (BVI) Limited issues USDY today. Ondo I LP and its GP, and SEC-registered Ondo Capital Management, make up OUSG's structure.
USDY (a secured note), OUSG (a fund or limited-partnership interest) and their rebasing wrappers are securities, not payment stablecoins.
Asset-management and advisory income, product income and spreads, and distribution and tokenization services.
Offering terms, OndoID (its identity check), transfer limits, custody and collateral agents, bridge controls and adviser decisions.
Treasury and fund assets, Ankura and other agents, custodians, conversion through Circle and Coinbase, blockchains and eligible investors.
Collateral that earns yield and a cash-management asset that can be swapped for stablecoins and used in DeFi (decentralized finance).
Normally converted into payment money first. Direct payment use is limited by securities eligibility rules and transfer controls.
The GENIUS Act excludes securities, so USDY and OUSG fall outside the payment-stablecoin definition.
Some product and blockchain integrations are live. Where descriptions of the issuer conflict, the current legal terms control.
How far tokenized securities can go into checkout, collateral and card products while keeping securities controls.
An issuer, agent or custodian problem, market loss, eligibility failure, bridge or control bug, or redemption delay.
A dollar-like net asset value (NAV) or instant conversion does not make the security a payment stablecoin.

rows.title: Morpho's vault curators decide where lenders' money goes, doing the intermediary's job
fields: open lending markets anyone can create and curator-managed vaults live

Morpho Association runs interfaces and ecosystem services. Morpho Labs is a separate development company. Control is split among governance and product-specific actors, across lending markets that cannot be changed and separately managed vaults.
Lending markets anyone can create, how vault money is allocated, and which yields are chosen
Governance cannot pause or rewrite existing Morpho markets. Vault owners, curators, allocators and sentinels can choose markets, allocate funds and use limited product powers.

Morpho Association is a French nonprofit association. Morpho Labs is a separate development company. Token governance, market creators and independent vault curators, allocators and sentinels are separate actors.
The underlying stablecoin is still owed by its issuer. The lender's or vault's receipt becomes a separate credit claim.
Borrowing interest, curator and vault fees, protocol rewards, and income from interfaces and integrations.
Market settings, choice of price oracle, vault curation and allocation, caps, guardians and distribution through front ends.
Stablecoin issuers, borrowers, collateral, price oracles, liquidators, curators and wallet and card distributors.
A source of yield increasingly built into institutional wallets and Stripe/Privy-style products.
A card or wallet sells, borrows against or moves a Morpho position into spendable money before the merchant is paid.
A Morpho receipt or vault claim needs its own analysis. The base payment coin's issuer status does not protect the yield product.
Watch curator concentration and whether card and wallet integrations reach production.
Which legal entity owes users in curated products, how bad debt is shared out and who controls emergency actions.
Bad debt, oracle failure, curator or allocation error, lack of liquidity, a flaw in a market that cannot be changed, a smart-contract exploit, or a front-end or custody failure.
Anyone can create a market, but that does not mean every vault is unmanaged or equally safe.

rows.title: M^0 shows clearly who controls minting, but not who owes holders
fields: M protocol live · unclear who owes ordinary holders
Protocol governance assigns minter, validator and earner roles. Each product's minters hold collateral in SPVs (special purpose vehicles).
Minting only by approved minters, confirmation of collateral, and programmable sharing of earnings
Governance can approve or remove roles. Validators can freeze minters and cancel mint proposals. MinterGateway controls minting and burning on the blockchain.

M^0 Foundation is a Swiss foundation that supports governance and ecosystem infrastructure. It is not automatically the issuer of every coin. Independent minters, SPVs, validators, earners, Stablecoin Core issuers and Extension administrators have separate responsibilities.
The M base token can have fixed or rebasing (self-adjusting) balances. Branded extensions can add another liability and distribution layer.
Interest that minters owe, payouts to earners, protocol and governance income, and branded-issuance services.
Approved lists for each role, validator attestations and freezes, MinterGateway contracts, each product's Stablecoin Core, Extension admins, bridges, the rate model and distribution vaults.
Minters staying solvent, SPV collateral, validators, custodians, governance and distributors.
Back-end money system for branded coins and balances that earn in the same token.
Usually through a branded distributor or processor, not with M as a visible retail asset.
A clear control system does not by itself name one legal entity that owes redemption. Yield paid in the same token complicates payment classification.
Product-specific legal documents are the deciding piece still missing.
Who owes ordinary M holders regular money, who owns the collateral, and how failures are resolved across minters.
A minter or SPV default, a wrong attestation, too few validators in control, a gateway bug or a governance failure.
Being able to switch issuers technically does not move the legal duty to redeem, the reserve property or the user contract. One token contract does not create one issuer for everyone.

rows.title: Agora keeps AUSD reserves in a segregated account, but its loyalty rewards are disputed
fields: AUSD live outside the U.S. · national trust bank proposed
AUSD issuance and a white-label platform for partner-branded coins. The proposed U.S. trust is a separate future entity.
Minting and redemption for corporate users, a segregated reserve, token administration and distribution through partners
Under its terms, Agora can freeze addresses, pause or upgrade, seize or destroy tokens, and choose how to treat chains and forks.
Agora Bermuda Limited acts for the AUSD Segregated Account. The proposed Agora National Trust Bank is not the current issuer.
AUSD is the base coin. Partner-branded coins may be separate obligations. Loyalty payouts add more AUSD rather than a wrapper token.
Reserve income, platform and white-label income, and loyalty distributions.
Onboarding verified corporate users, reserve policy, token administration, partner contracts and reward terms.
State Street/VanEck and other reserve providers, banks and custodians, blockchains and verified distributors.
A base coin that looks regulated, used across multiple blockchains and partner protocols.
Needs an eligible distributor or processor. Only verified corporate users can redeem directly.
May move to a new issuer. But balance-based loyalty rewards paid in AUSD need close review under issuer-yield limits.
The national trust bank is proposed, not current. The binding terms control over what product pages say.
The final U.S. issuer, who pays rewards and on what basis, and what partner coins legally promise.
Reserve or custodian problem, delayed redemption or payout in assets instead of cash, token-admin action, or confusion over partner obligations.
Agora does not automatically redeem a partner coin just because it is backed by access to AUSD.

rows.title: Liquity's core contracts have no administrator, so they cannot be paused or upgraded
fields: BOLD and LUSD live · core contracts cannot be changed
Liquity AG develops and supports the software. Core contracts that cannot be changed run borrowing, redemptions and liquidations, with no administrator who can upgrade them.
Borrowing against more collateral than the loan, and redemption for crypto collateral
The core design has no way to pause, upgrade, blacklist or move by governance vote. Front ends and third parties can still restrict access.

Liquity AG develops and supports software but does not run one official front end. Independent interfaces, the unchangeable contracts, and users and liquidators are separate. No named issuer that owes regular money is documented.
BOLD and LUSD are protocol debt assets. Stability Pool positions are separate.
Borrower interest, gains from liquidations, Stability Pool returns and activity on third-party interfaces.
Core contract rules, collateral types fixed at launch, user positions, liquidators and independent interfaces.
Ethereum, outside collateral and liquid staking token (LST) issuers, oracles and market liquidity, liquidators and front ends.
A protocol dollar strongly built to resist censorship. It fits poorly with institutions' expectation that coins follow lawful orders.
Must be swapped on the market for a coin a processor supports.
Strong case that it falls outside the payment-stablecoin definition. Permitted-issuer compliance would need a successor system.
Any structural compliance change must come in new contracts or products, not a retrofit of the existing ones.
How the law treats unchangeable protocols, and practical distribution when intermediaries keep approved lists.
Collateral, oracle or liquidity failure, chain disruption or interfaces disappearing. No administrator can step in to rescue it.
Unchangeable contracts do not remove sanctions, interface, collateral-issuer or market risk.

fields: The Department of the Treasury (Treasury) is issuing this advance notice of proposed rulemaking (ANPRM) to solicit public comment on questions relating to the implementation of the Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins (GENIUS) Act. The GENIUS Act tasks Treasury (and various other federal agencies) with issuing regulations that encourage innovation in payment stablecoins while also providing an appropriately tailored regime to protect consumers, mitigate potential illicit finance risks, and address financial stability risks. Through this ANPRM, Treasury is seeking public comment on potential regulations that may be promulgated by Treasury, including regarding regulatory clarity, prohibitions on certain issuances and marketing, Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) anti-money laundering (AML) and sanctions obligations, the balance of state-level oversight with federal oversight, comparable foreign regulatory and supervisory regimes, and tax issues, among other things. Treasury is seeking comment on all aspects of the ANPRM from all interested parties and also requests commenters to identify other issues that Treasury should consider.

fields: The NCUA Board (Board) is seeking comment on proposed regulations to implement portions of the Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins Act (GENIUS Act). The GENIUS Act charges the NCUA with licensing, regulating, and supervising payment stablecoin issuers that are subsidiaries of federally insured credit unions (FICU subsidiaries). The GENIUS Act also requires the NCUA to issue implementing regulations by July 18th, 2026. This proposed rule proposes regulations to implement the statutorily required process for approval and licensure of permitted payment stablecoin issuers (PPSIs) subject to the NCUA's jurisdiction. A forthcoming proposal will propose regulations to implement the standards and restrictions imposed by the GENIUS Act on PPSIs.
